chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Ibn Al-Azramy, with an unbroken chain, said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) was asked about the clouds, where they are. He said: They are on trees, on dunes, on the shore of the sea, taking refuge there. So when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intends to send them, He sends a wind which stirs them, and appoints angels over them who strike them with 'makhariq' (thunderclaps/strikers), and that is lightning, so they rise up.
It is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir the clouds and spread them in the sky...
And the angel's name is Al-Ra'd (Thunder).
ai.seo_question: Where do clouds come from according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this cosmological narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) describes the physical resting place of clouds on terrestrial features like trees and dunes, illustrating a pre-modern understanding of meteorology rooted in divine agency. The text highlights the role of angels, specifically naming the angel of thunder, who manipulate the clouds using 'makhariq' (threshing flails) to generate lightning, thereby linking natural phenomena directly to celestial intervention. This account underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the tangible, physical nature of the unseen world and the continuous involvement of angels in sustaining creation.
